blocks.text: Imagine multiple users trying to book the last seat on a flight at the same time. How do databases ensure that only one booking is successful?

blocks.markdown: Concurrency control is a critical aspect of database systems, ensuring that transactions are executed in a safe and efficient manner even when multiple users access the database simultaneously. This unit explores common anomalies, the concept of serialisability, and the mechanisms used to maintain data integrity.

blocks.title: Transaction
blocks.text: A transaction is a sequence of database operations that are treated as a single unit. It must be atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable (ACID properties).

blocks.markdown: When multiple transactions are executed concurrently, anomalies such as lost updates, dirty reads, and non-repeatable reads can occur. These anomalies can lead to inconsistent database states.

blocks.title: Lost Update
blocks.text: A lost update occurs when two transactions read the same data and then update it, with the second update overwriting the first.

blocks.title: Dirty Read
blocks.text: A dirty read happens when a transaction reads data that has been modified by another transaction that has not yet been committed.

blocks.title: Non-repeatable Read
blocks.text: A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction reads the same data twice and gets different values because another transaction has modified the data in between the reads.

blocks.markdown: To manage these anomalies, databases use concurrency control mechanisms. One such mechanism is locking.

blocks.title: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
blocks.text: Two-Phase Locking is a concurrency control method that ensures serialisability by dividing the execution of a transaction into two phases: a growing phase, where locks can be acquired but not released, and a shrinking phase, where locks can be released but not acquired.

blocks.title: Understanding Two-Phase Locking
blocks.prompt: Consider two transactions, T1 and T2, accessing a shared resource. T1 locks and updates the resource, then T2 attempts to lock the same resource. Explain how 2PL ensures serialisability.

steps.text: T1 enters the growing phase and acquires a lock on the resource.
T1 updates the resource and then enters the shrinking phase, releasing the lock.
T2 can only acquire the lock after T1 has released it, ensuring that T2's operations follow T1's in a serial order.

blocks.answer: Two-Phase Locking ensures that transactions are executed in a serial order by controlling when locks can be acquired and released, preventing interleaving that could lead to anomalies.

blocks.markdown: Different isolation levels in databases allow for varying degrees of concurrency and consistency. These levels are defined by the anomalies they permit.

rows: Dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads
blocks.caption: Comparison of Isolation Levels and Permitted Anomalies

blocks.title: Comparing Isolation Levels
blocks.prompt: A database transaction is executed under the 'Read Committed' isolation level. Identify the anomalies that can occur and explain why.

steps.text: Under 'Read Committed', a transaction can only read committed data, preventing dirty reads.
However, non-repeatable reads can occur because data can be modified by other transactions between reads.
Phantom reads can also occur because new rows can be added by other transactions.

blocks.answer: Under 'Read Committed', non-repeatable reads and phantom reads can occur because transactions can read committed data that may change before the transaction is complete.

points: Concurrency control is essential for maintaining data integrity in multi-user environments.
Two-Phase Locking ensures serialisability by controlling lock acquisition and release.
Different isolation levels balance concurrency and consistency by permitting certain anomalies.
